title: Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure
description: Federal appellate procedure from a district court disposition through direct appeal, briefing, argument, merits decision, rehearing, and certiorari to the Supreme Court — tracking FRAP jurisdictional deadlines, standards of review, and the Bowles v. Russell trap.
jurisdiction: Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure / U.S. Courts of Appeals

nodes.label: District Court Order or Judgment Entered
nodes.note: Entry of a district court judgment or order marks the gateway moment for appellate jurisdiction. Not every order triggers appeal rights — the order must fall within one of the narrow statutory categories. Miscategorizing an order (treating an interlocutory order as final, or vice versa) cascades into jurisdictional dismissal downstream, regardless of merit.

nodes.label: Is the Order a Final Judgment?
nodes.note: The finality inquiry is mechanical but requires precision: a final decision must dispose of all claims as to all parties, or be certified under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b). Many seemingly conclusive orders fail the test because they leave pending counterclaims, third-party claims, or unresolved damages issues. Appealing too early results in dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Final Judgment
nodes.note: A true final judgment ends the district court's power over the case on the merits and triggers the 30-day appeal clock. The judgment must resolve the entire controversy between the parties. Partial judgments, conditional orders, and orders that reserve jurisdiction (e.g., to tax costs or award attorney fees) may fail the finality test and block immediate appeal.

nodes.label: Interlocutory Order
nodes.note: An interlocutory order does not end the litigation on the merits and thus falls outside the default appeal-of-right gate under § 1291. Section 1292 creates three narrow exceptions, but the default assumption is that an interlocutory order is not appealable. Trying to appeal without qualifying through one of the three doors results in dismissal.

nodes.label: Interlocutory Review Door Available?
nodes.cite: 28 U.S.C. §§ 1292(a)-(b); Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp., 337 U.S. 541 (1949)
nodes.note: Three doors strictly govern interlocutory review: first, § 1292(a)(1) injunction/receivership orders (as of right); second, the collateral order doctrine (Cohen test requiring three conjunctive factors); third, § 1292(b) permissive certification (requires district court consent and substantial ground for difference of opinion). Missing all three means no appeal — litigation continues until final judgment.

nodes.label: Interlocutory Order Ripe for Appeal
nodes.note: Whichever door got you here, the downstream notice-of-appeal mechanics are identical to a final-judgment appeal. The narrow jurisdictional gate is passed; the 30-day notice-of-appeal deadline and standard briefing rules now apply.

nodes.label: No Appellate Jurisdiction — Await Final Judgment
nodes.note: This is the normal posture for most interlocutory orders: simply not appealable. Litigation continues below and the appellant must await a final judgment to seek review. This is not a trap — it is the designed statutory default. Attempting to appeal will be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Notice of Appeal Window Open
nodes.note: The appeal deadline is jurisdictional and non-waivable under Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007). Civil cases have 30 days (60 if the U.S., a U.S. agency, or officer is a party); criminal defendants have 14 days. Missing this deadline strips appellate jurisdiction permanently.

nodes.label: Notice of Appeal Filed
nodes.note: The notice must specify the party taking the appeal, designate the judgment/order appealed from, and identify the court to which the appeal is taken. Courts construe informal notices liberally per Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962), unless the defect is fatal (wrong party or judgment).

nodes.label: Rule 4(a)(4) Tolling Motion Filed
nodes.note: Motions for judgment as a matter of law, new trial, amended findings, altered/amended judgment, and certain Rule 60(b) motions toll the appeal clock when filed within their own FRCP deadlines (typically 28 days). A motion filed one day after the FRCP deadline does not toll.

nodes.label: Tolling Motion Disposed
nodes.note: The full appeal period runs anew from the entry of the order disposing of the last remaining tolling motion. If multiple tolling motions are pending, the clock does not restart until the final one is decided.

nodes.label: DISMISSED — Untimely Notice of Appeal (Jurisdictional)
nodes.cite: Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007); 28 U.S.C. § 2107; FRAP 4(a)
nodes.note: PERMADEATH. A statutory appeal deadline is strictly jurisdictional and cannot be waived, excused, or extended by equitable principle. Even a district court order purporting to extend the deadline is void ab initio. Loss of jurisdiction is irrevocable.

nodes.label: Notice of Appeal Contents Deficient
nodes.cite: FRAP 3(c)(1), (4)-(5); Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962); Smith v. Barry, 502 U.S. 244 (1992); Torres v. Oakland Scavenger Co., 487 U.S. 312 (1988)
nodes.note: Courts apply liberal construction to informal notices where the intent to appeal is objectively clear (Foman/Smith line). However, naming the wrong party, wrong judgment, or wrong court may be jurisdictionally fatal and incurable, even if intent is clear (Torres).

nodes.label: Motion to Extend or Reopen Time
nodes.note: FRAP 4(a)(5) allows the district court to extend time up to 30 additional days for excusable neglect or good cause. FRAP 4(a)(6) allows reopening for 14 days for lack of notice of entry (motion filed within 14 days of actual notice, no later than 180 days after entry). Both carry absolute outer limits.

nodes.label: Appeal Docketed
nodes.note: The district clerk transmits the notice to the court of appeals clerk, who dockets the appeal and assigns a case number. Docketing is ministerial; appellate jurisdiction attaches when the notice is filed in the district court, not when docketed in the appellate court.

nodes.label: Appellee Considers a Cross-Appeal
nodes.note: A party wishing to attack a judgment (not merely defend it against the appellant's arguments) must file its own notice of cross-appeal. A cross-appeal asserts a separate basis for reversal or a request that the court award a more favorable judgment to the cross-appellant than the district court gave.

nodes.label: Notice of Cross-Appeal Filed
nodes.note: Due within 14 days after the first notice of appeal, or the otherwise-applicable Rule 4(a)(1) period, whichever is later. The deadline is non-extendable under the plain text of the rule — missing it forecloses cross-appellate relief.

nodes.label: No Cross-Appeal — Judgment Defended Only
nodes.cite: FRAP 4(a)(3); United States v. American Railway Express Co., 265 U.S. 425 (1924)
nodes.note: Without a cross-appeal, a party cannot argue for reversal or a more favorable judgment on appeal. The party is confined to defending the judgment on existing grounds or alternative theories, but cannot affirmatively seek relief — this is the binding cross-appeal constraint.

nodes.label: Parties Consider Dismissing the Appeal
nodes.note: By stipulation of all parties (with costs as agreed) or on the appellant's own motion — courts almost always grant such dismissals unless compelling institutional interests (e.g., class certification, precedential impact) require retention of the case.

nodes.label: Appeal Voluntarily Dismissed
nodes.note: On dismissal, the underlying district court judgment stands undisturbed unless the dismissal order provides otherwise (e.g., with prejudice, without prejudice, or conditional). Voluntary dismissal typically reflects settlement and does not resolve the merits — it is neither a win nor a loss on appeal.

nodes.label: Transcript Needed?
nodes.note: Appellant must decide within 14 days of the notice of appeal whether to order the transcript. Ordering creates an enforceable duty on the court reporter to transcribe and file; failure to order by the deadline doesn't waive the opportunity to appeal, but will delay the record and potentially prejudice waiver arguments if the record remains incomplete.

nodes.label: Transcript Ordered
nodes.note: Written order must be filed with the district clerk; appellant arranges payment with the reporter at the time of ordering. If ordering only a partial transcript, appellant must designate issues on appeal, and appellee then has 14 days to designate additional portions — refusal to order those portions gives appellee grounds to seek a court order compelling appellant to do so, shifting cost and timeline control from appellant to appellee.

nodes.label: Agreed Statement in Lieu of Transcript
nodes.note: Agreed statement must be signed by both parties and contain only facts 'essential to the court's resolution of the issues' — neither party may later expand it mid-appeal to contest completeness. The statement still requires district court approval before certification, creating a procedural gate. Missing the district court's approval forecloses this pathway and forces a return to transcript ordering.

nodes.label: Record on Appeal Complete and Transmitted
nodes.note: The record is 'complete' when the transcript is filed (or agreed statement approved) and the district clerk has numbered and transmitted all original papers to the appellate clerk. The reporter's duty is to note receipt and file within 30 days; delays beyond 30 days require a reporter request for extension (not appellant's action), and failure to report timely triggers mandatory circuit-to-district notification, shifting the compliance burden to the trial judge.

nodes.label: Move to Stay Judgment Pending Appeal?
nodes.note: Mandatory exhaustion: must apply to the district court first under FRAP 8(a)(1)(A). Only if the district court denies relief or cannot act may the movant apply to the court of appeals. FRAP 27 governs the form of all appellate motions generally (10-day response, single-judge or panel action) — many appellants shortcut the district-court step, forfeiting the venue best positioned to assess likelihood of reversal and irreparable harm.

nodes.label: Stay Granted — Enforcement Suspended
nodes.note: Stay is almost always conditioned on a supersedeas bond equal to the judgment plus interest and costs. The bond requirement is the real control gate — inability to post money kills the stay in practice, regardless of legal merit on the appeal.

nodes.label: Stay Denied — Judgment Enforceable
nodes.note: Judgment becomes executable while the appeal is pending. Critical trap: if the appellee executes and collects before reversal, the appellant's only remedy is replevin or an action against the judgment creditor — reversal does not automatically restore collected funds.

nodes.label: Appellant's Opening Brief Due
nodes.note: The 40-day deadline runs from the date the record is filed with the court, not from the notice of appeal. Appellant must track the actual record closure date to avoid confusion; missing this self-inflicted trap is a leading cause of appellate dismissal. FRAP 28(a) sets required contents; FRAP 32(a)(7) caps the brief at 13,000 words (or 30 pages if monospaced).

nodes.label: Opening Brief Filed
nodes.note: The opening brief frames the issues, selects the standard of review, and defines the factual universe for appellate review. The appellant is bound by these choices; the reply brief cannot resurrect abandoned arguments, and new theories in reply are waived. The 13,000-word cap forces ruthless economy in issue-spotting.

nodes.label: DISMISSED — Failure to Prosecute (No Opening Brief)
nodes.note: Dismissal for 'want of prosecution' when the appellant fails to file timely is discretionary with the court but nearly automatic on appellee motion. This is a conduct-based sanction, not a jurisdictional defect, and is extremely difficult to revive post-dismissal because it reflects lack of diligence, not legal error.

nodes.label: Appellee's Response Brief Filed
nodes.note: The appellee enjoys asymmetric freedom: it may defend the judgment on any ground in the record without admitting any fact or standard the appellant proposed, and may attack the appellant's statement of the case or standard of review without conceding issue-framing. The 30-day period runs from service of the opening brief and can be extended for good cause.

nodes.label: Appellant's Reply Brief Filed
nodes.note: The reply brief is optional — failure to file waives no substantive right, but filing one that strays beyond the appellee's response opens waiver traps. The 6,500-word cap is non-negotiable; new arguments, new authorities, and arguments not fairly responsive to the response brief are all waived.

nodes.label: Briefing Closed
nodes.note: Once all briefs are filed or the reply deadline expires, the written record closes and is fixed. No supplemental briefs are permitted absent extraordinary circumstances (e.g., intervening Supreme Court authority). The panel's decision is now constrained to the four corners of the briefs and the certified record on appeal.

nodes.label: Oral Argument or Submission on Briefs?
nodes.note: Panel discretion to grant or dispense with oral argument — litigant expectations often misaligned with actual practice. Argument is dispensed with only when the panel unanimously agrees the appeal is frivolous, the dispositive issues are authoritatively decided, or the briefs adequately present the facts and legal arguments.

nodes.label: Oral Argument Held
nodes.note: Typical 15-minute per-side allocation (circuit-specific variations apply). Panels use argument to test weak points in the briefs; oral argument is not a second chance to rewrite a losing brief but rather to address judicial concerns flagged during panel circulation.

nodes.label: Submitted on the Briefs
nodes.note: Merits decided solely on written briefs without live argument — far more common in high-volume circuits than litigants anticipate. Decision occurs with no opportunity for live response to judicial questioning or hidden panel concerns revealed only in the opinion.

nodes.label: Which Standard of Review Governs?
nodes.note: The single most outcome-determinative procedural fork — identical facts and panel composition yield opposite affirm/reverse outcomes depending on whether the ruling implicates questions of law, discretion, or fact. Standard selection is rarely contestable once the issue category is fixed.

nodes.label: De Novo Review (Questions of Law)
nodes.cite: Pure questions of law standard; see United States v. Ionia Management S.A., 555 U.S. 99 (2012) for contract interpretation; Ornelas v. United States, 517 U.S. 690 (1996) for mixed questions
nodes.note: No deference to the district court's legal conclusions — decided fresh. Includes summary judgment grants, dismissals, statutory interpretation. Highest reversal rate of the three standards. (The blueprint's originally proposed cite, Salve Regina Dockery Co. v. Russell, could not be verified and has been replaced with the established de novo authorities above.)

nodes.label: Abuse-of-Discretion Review (Discretionary Rulings)
nodes.cite: Cooter & Gell v. Hartmarx Corp., 496 U.S. 384 (1990)
nodes.note: Governs evidentiary rulings, discovery orders, sanctions, case management. Reversed only for wrong legal standard, clearly erroneous facts, or a decision no reasonable judge could reach.

nodes.label: Clear-Error Review (Factual Findings)
nodes.cite: FRCP 52(a)(6); Anderson v. City of Bessemer City, 470 U.S. 564 (1985)
nodes.note: Most deferential standard — reversal requires a 'definite and firm conviction that a mistake has been committed,' even if the panel would have decided differently. Especially deferential to credibility findings.

nodes.label: AFFIRMED
nodes.note: Judgment stands because no reversible error was found, but 'affirmed' need not mean the court agreed with the district court's reasoning — it only means the outcome was legally permissible. The real trap is assuming the panel endorsed the lower court's reasoning.

nodes.label: REVERSED
nodes.note: Final reversal with judgment entered — the panel disagreed on the merits and imposed its own definitive holding without remand. Relatively rare in civil practice because most reversals require factfinding or application-of-law tasks unsuited to appellate authority.

nodes.label: REVERSED AND REMANDED
nodes.note: The standard reversal posture: the panel identifies the wrong legal rule or standard applied below, vacates judgment, and returns the case for the district court to redecide under the correct rule. This is the most common reversal outcome.

nodes.label: VACATED AND REMANDED
nodes.note: Doesn't necessarily hold the district court wrong on the merits — often signals a procedural defect, intervening change in law, or need for further fact-finding. The trap: this outcome looks like reversal but gives the district court wide latitude on remand.

nodes.label: AFFIRMED IN PART, REVERSED IN PART
nodes.note: Common in multi-claim or multi-party appeals decided claim-by-claim under different standards of review — a genuine mixed result, not a compromise. Each part stands on its own legal footing.

nodes.label: Seek Rehearing?
nodes.note: After judgment entry, parties have 14 days (or 45 if the U.S. is a party) to file a petition for panel rehearing, en banc rehearing, or both in a combined petition. Most circuits treat the deadline as firm. Filing preserves the issue and tolls the 90-day certiorari clock under Supreme Court Rule 13.3.

nodes.label: Petition for Rehearing / Rehearing En Banc Filed
nodes.note: The petition must comply with FRAP 32 formatting and cannot exceed 3,900 words (computer-generated) or 15 pages (typewritten). For panel rehearing, it must identify specific overlooked legal or factual points; for en banc, it must show a conflict with another circuit, an intra-circuit conflict, conflict with Supreme Court precedent, or a question of exceptional importance.

nodes.label: Panel Rules on Rehearing
nodes.note: The panel rules on the petition; no fixed FRAP deadline exists, though circuit practice generally resolves it in under 40 days. Grant rates are extremely low; panels rarely reverse their own decisions absent a substantial legal or factual error. No response is permitted unless the court requests one.

nodes.label: Active Judges Vote on En Banc Rehearing
nodes.note: All active judges of the circuit vote on whether to order en banc rehearing; a majority of active judges must vote in favor to grant. FRAP 40(c) provides that 'unless a judge calls for a vote, a vote need not be taken' — the court may dispose of the petition without a formal poll, effectively a denial. En banc rehearing is extraordinarily rare, reserved for circuit splits or truly exceptional questions.

nodes.label: Rehearing Granted — Opinion Amended or Reheard
nodes.note: When panel rehearing is granted, the panel may dispose of the case without further briefing, order supplemental briefing or argument, or issue other appropriate orders. For en banc rehearing, the panel opinion is vacated entirely and the case is reargued before all active judges.

nodes.label: Rehearing and Rehearing En Banc Both Denied (Final)
nodes.note: Once both panel and en banc petitions are denied (or the deadline to file them passes without filing), the original panel decision is final at the circuit level. The mandate issues 7 days after the later of expiration of the petition period or entry of the order denying it. The 90-day certiorari deadline now runs from this denial.

nodes.label: Mandate Issues
nodes.note: The mandate is the formal order returning jurisdiction to the district court — distinct from the opinion and critical for enforcing the judgment. It issues automatically 7 days after either expiration of the rehearing period or denial of a timely rehearing petition. The mandate, not the opinion, is what actually binds the district court.

nodes.label: Mandate Stayed Pending Certiorari
nodes.note: On motion, the court of appeals may stay its mandate pending a cert petition — otherwise the district court could enforce the judgment while the Supreme Court is still deciding whether to take the case. The stay is discretionary and requires a showing of likelihood of cert grant plus irreparable harm.

nodes.label: Certiorari Petition Window
nodes.note: 90 days from entry of judgment or from denial of a timely rehearing petition — not extendable except by a single application to a Circuit Justice for good cause, filed before the deadline expires.

nodes.label: FINAL — Certiorari Not Sought
nodes.note: The vast majority of court of appeals decisions end here — no petition filed, judgment final and unreviewable by any federal court.

nodes.label: Petition for Certiorari Filed
nodes.note: Governed by the 'rule of four' — cert is granted on the vote of any four Justices, not a majority. Discretionary review, not a matter of right; the petition must meet one of the Rule 10 criteria (typically a circuit split, an important federal question, or conflict with Supreme Court precedent).

nodes.label: Supreme Court Grants or Denies Certiorari
nodes.note: The Supreme Court grants certiorari to only about 1% of petitions. Most petitions receive zero substantive review; the Court's denial is typically summary and involves only a screening review by law clerks. No opinions are issued on the merits of denied petitions.

nodes.label: CERT DENIED (Final)
nodes.note: A denial of certiorari is not a ruling on the merits and carries zero precedential weight — parties cannot cite a cert denial as support for any legal proposition, and the denial expresses no view on the correctness of the lower court's decision.

nodes.label: CERT GRANTED — Case Transfers to the Supreme Court
nodes.note: Once certiorari is granted, the case is removed from the court of appeals docket and briefing proceeds under the Supreme Court's own rules, not FRAP. This pack's jurisdiction over the case ends here.

edges.label: Injunction order — appeal as of right

deadline.extensionAuthority: Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)(5)
deadline.note: Appeal of right from injunction/receivership orders. Notice of appeal due within 30 days of entry, extendable to 60 days maximum under FRAP 4(a)(5). Missing the deadline strips appellate jurisdiction regardless of merit.

edges.label: Order meets collateral order doctrine
edges.authority: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp., 337 U.S. 541 (1949)

deadline.extensionAuthority: Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)(5)
deadline.note: Collateral order doctrine requires all three Cohen factors: (1) conclusively determines a disputed question; (2) resolves an important issue separate from the merits; (3) unreviewable on appeal from final judgment. Same 30-day deadline as statutory appeals.

deadline.extensionAuthority: Fed. R. App. P. 5(a)(3)
deadline.note: Permissive appeal. District court must certify substantial ground for difference of opinion within 10 days of entry (FRAP 5(a)(1)); applicant then has 10 days to apply to the appellate court (FRAP 5(a)(3)). Neither deadline is extendable.

deadline.extensionAuthority: Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)(5)
deadline.note: Notice of appeal due within 30 days of entry of final judgment, extendable to 60 days maximum under FRAP 4(a)(5). Deadline is jurisdictional; missing it by even one day strips appellate court of jurisdiction. Post-judgment motions may alter the triggering date under FRAP 4(a)(4).

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 4(a)(5) (may extend up to 30 additional days only via motion before expiration)
deadline.note: If notice is not filed within 30 days, the appeal is untimely. Under Bowles, no equitable exception or late filing is permitted — appellate jurisdiction is lost permanently and cannot be restored.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 4(a)(5) (may extend up to 30 additional days only via motion before expiration)
deadline.note: When the U.S., a U.S. agency, or an officer acting in official capacity is a party, the deadline is 60 days. Missing this deadline forecloses appellate jurisdiction entirely under 28 U.S.C. § 2107.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 4(b)(4) (may be extended for excusable neglect or good cause, subject to Bowles jurisdictional limit)
deadline.note: Criminal defendants have only 14 days to file notice of appeal. A late notice — even one day late — is untimely and strips appellate jurisdiction; no exception for prosecutor's error or trial counsel's mistake.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRCP 6(b) may extend the tolling-motion deadline by up to 28 days total (only for FRCP 50(b), 59(e), 60(b) motions)
deadline.note: Tolling motions must be filed within the FRCP deadline (e.g., 28 days for a FRCP 59(e) motion for new trial). A tolling motion filed even one day late does not restart the appeal clock.

edges.label: District court rules on the motion

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 4(a)(5) (extension may apply to the restarted deadline)
deadline.note: The full appeal period runs anew from the date the order disposing of the last tolling motion is entered. A new 30-day clock (or 60-day if U.S. party) begins; missing this deadline is fatal.

edges.label: Court excuses the technical defect
edges.authority: Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962); Smith v. Barry, 502 U.S. 244 (1992); FRAP 3(e)

edges.label: Defect held jurisdictional, uncurable
edges.authority: Torres v. Oakland Scavenger Co., 487 U.S. 312 (1988); FRAP 3(c)

edges.label: Move to extend or reopen deadline

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 4(a)(5)(A) (court may extend if motion filed before deadline expires); FRAP 4(a)(6) (may reopen for 14 days if lack of notice of entry)
deadline.note: A party may file a motion to extend time to appeal before the deadline expires. The district court may grant up to 30 additional days for excusable neglect or good cause. A motion filed after the deadline expires may only invoke FRAP 4(a)(6) (reopening).

14 days after the first notice of appeal, or within the original FRAP 4(a)(1) period, whichever is later. Missing this deadline forecloses the cross-appeal entirely — no equitable exceptions or late filing allowed.

edges.label: Stipulate to or move for dismissal

deadline.note: No extension is available for the 14-day ordering deadline; missing it leaves the appellant with only the option to seek appellate relief on an inadequate record, or risk abandonment of issues not covered by existing papers.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 11(b) (reporter may request extension for completion beyond 30 days; no formal party motion needed)
deadline.note: Reporter has 30 days from receipt of the order to file the transcript with the district clerk. Requests for additional time are filed with the circuit clerk. Failure to file timely triggers circuit-clerk notice to the trial judge and risks sanction if the record becomes unavailable.

edges.label: Move for stay pending appeal — granted

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 26(b); court order
deadline.note: 10-day response period (FRAP 27(a)(3)) applies to all motions, including a motion to stay. Failure to meet the deadline may result in the motion being deemed submitted without response, waiver of oral argument, or denial.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 26(b); court order
deadline.note: Same 10-day response period applies. Missing the deadline for opposition may result in default or deemed abandonment of objections.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 26(b); court discretion for good cause
deadline.note: Failure to file by day 40 (or the extended date) permits an appellee motion to dismiss for want of prosecution under FRAP 31(c), triggering a dismissal that is nearly impossible to revive.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 26(b); court discretion for good cause
deadline.note: Appellee's failure to file within 30 days is grounds for default, but the appellee retains the right to oral argument by court permission even if the brief is late; missing this deadline is far less terminal than the appellant's miss.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 26(b); court discretion for good cause; FRAP 31(a)(1) requires filing at least 7 days before argument
deadline.note: Reply brief must be filed at least 7 days before oral argument (if scheduled) or risk rejection. Late reply briefs are rarely accepted; this is a cascading deadline that depends on the argument calendar, not a pure 21-day rule.

edges.label: Issue is a question of law
edges.authority: Pure questions of law (statutory construction, constitutional interpretation, legal standards for admissibility)

edges.label: Issue is a discretionary ruling
edges.authority: Cooter & Gell v. Hartmarx Corp., 496 U.S. 384 (1990)

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 40(a)(1); circuit local rules may allow additional extensions by panel order or stipulation
deadline.note: Losing party must file a petition for panel rehearing or rehearing en banc within 14 days of judgment entry. Missing this deadline forecloses appellate-level recourse (except discretionary certiorari); the appellate judgment becomes final.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 40(a)(1); circuit local rules
deadline.note: Losing party (the party who prevailed below) must file a petition for rehearing within 14 days or lose appellate-level recourse. Extension requires a proactive panel request or stipulation — default expiration is strict.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 40(a)(1); circuit local rules
deadline.note: Either party may file a petition for rehearing (the appellee who won on appeal may seek en banc review; the appellant who still faces remand may challenge the legal standard applied). Missing the 14-day window forecloses the petition and accelerates remand.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 40(a)(1); circuit local rules
deadline.note: Either party may petition for rehearing if they contest the panel's reasoning for vacatur or seek clarification of the remand instructions. Missing the 14-day deadline leaves only the (weaker) remand process to raise objections.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 40(a)(1); circuit local rules
deadline.note: Both parties may have grounds for rehearing: the party who lost on the reversed portion may challenge the legal rule; the party who won only on the affirmed portion may seek full reversal. A single 14-day deadline applies to the entire judgment.

deadline.extensionAuthority: FRAP 26(b) is silent on FRAP 40 deadlines; extension is theoretically possible for good cause but extremely rarely granted in practice
deadline.note: Missing the 14-day (or 45-day if the U.S. is a party) deadline forfeits the right to seek rehearing and loses the ability to toll the Supreme Court's 90-day certiorari clock under Rule 13.3.

If no rehearing petition is filed within 14 days (or 45 days for the U.S.), the time to petition expires and the mandate issues automatically 7 days thereafter. The 90-day Supreme Court certiorari clock then runs from the original judgment date.

edges.label: Panel denies — en banc poll proceeds
Majority votes to rehear en banc

deadline.note: After the amended opinion is filed (or the rehearing is disposed of), the mandate issues 7 days later. The amended opinion becomes the circuit's final judgment for purposes of the Supreme Court's 90-day certiorari deadline.

The mandate issues 7 days after the order denying rehearing and/or en banc rehearing, or 7 days after expiration of the petition deadline if no petition was timely filed. This triggers finality at the circuit level and starts the 90-day certiorari clock.

edges.label: Judgment final — cert clock runs
edges.authority: Fed. R. App. P. 41(b); Sup. Ct. R. 13.3

deadline.extensionAuthority: Sup. Ct. R. 13.6
deadline.note: The 90-day deadline is measured from the date the appellate opinion is filed/docketed. Missing this deadline forecloses any Supreme Court review; the judgment becomes final and enforceable. Extensions require filing before the deadline expires.

edges.label: Move to stay mandate for cert

deadline.extensionAuthority: Sup. Ct. R. 13.6
deadline.note: If cert is denied or the 90-day window expires (whichever is earlier), the stay terminates automatically and the mandate issues to enforce the judgment.

deadline.extensionAuthority: Sup. Ct. R. 13.3 (single application to Circuit Justice only)
deadline.note: Failure to file within 90 days permanently bars federal review; there is no tolling, no exceptions for attorney mistake, and no relief even if the court of appeals misled the parties about the deadline.
